**Deep Time**

In the Jack Hills of Western Australia, prospectors have found grains of zircon that crystallized 4.4 billion years ago—older than nearly any surviving rock on Earth, relics of a planet that has since melted, buckled, and remade itself many times over. Hold one between your fingers (it's smaller than a grain of sand) and you're touching something that formed before the oceans existed, before anything that could properly be called an *event*.

I return to facts like this not because they're impressive—though they are—but because of what they do to the imagination. Human intuition is built for seasons, lifespans, generations. Deep time breaks that machinery, and the breaking is strangely pleasurable, the way good vertigo is.

Consider: if Earth's history were compressed into a single day, life appears in the early morning hours, complex life around dinnertime, and all of recorded human history—every empire, every war, every love letter ever written—occupies the last sliver of a second before midnight. The dinosaurs had a longer run than the time separating them from us. Everything since their extinction could fit into the gap between two notes of a song.

And yet here's the part I love most: we can *know* any of this at all. The universe spent billions of years entirely unwitnessed—no observer, no record, just matter doing its slow work—and then, recently enough to be almost embarrassing, some arrangement of atoms on a minor planet started asking questions. We read isotopes like handwriting. We count tree rings and ice cores and sediment layers the way you'd read a stranger's diary. The rocks kept minutes of meetings nobody attended, and we arrived late and reconstructed the agenda anyway.

There's a version of this meant to make you feel insignificant, and I suppose it does, briefly. But mostly it makes me feel lucky in an almost absurd way. Of all the moments across 4.5 billion years, minds capable of wondering got scheduled *now*—late enough to inherit the whole archive, early enough that so much of it is still legible. We are the part of the universe that reads its own receipts.

Those zircon grains will outlast everything humanity has ever built. That's fine. They were never competing with us. They were just waiting, patiently, for someone small and temporary to pick them up, ask how old they were, and be genuinely astonished by the answer.
